report:
Conclusion: the claim is false. The strongest evidence does not show that induced abortion raises breast-cancer risk. NCI’s expert workshop review concluded that neither induced nor spontaneous abortion increases risk, while noting why the idea persists: early case–control studies were inconsistent and vulnerable to recall/underreporting bias and confounding by parity and age at first birth (https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/abortion-miscarriage-risk). ACOG likewise says early studies were methodologically flawed, while “more rigorous recent studies demonstrate no causal relationship” (https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2009/06/induced-abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk).

The pivotal evidence is the Collaborative Group reanalysis of individual data from 53 studies in 16 countries, about 83,000 women with breast cancer; it found no overall increase for spontaneous or induced abortion, and retrospective reports suggesting risk were not supported by prospective record-based data (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(04)15835-2/fulltext). Large registry cohorts such as Denmark’s reached the same result. Some small or subgroup findings appear occasionally, but they are inconsistent and often based on few cases. Bottom line: a full-term pregnancy has complex short- and long-term effects, but having an abortion itself has not been shown to increase subsequent breast-cancer risk.
